questions.q: Why does this lesson say rollback is often harder on Salesforce than on some other platforms?
options: Because metadata rollback can fail if other changes built on top of it, and data changes already made to records generally cannot be undone just by reverting metadata
Because Salesforce has no deployment tooling at all
Because Salesforce automatically rolls back every deployment after 24 hours
Because rollback is only a concern for Apex code, never for declarative changes
questions.explain: The lesson identifies two distinct problems: metadata rollback can be unclean if later changes depend on the new version, and data already changed by a deployed Flow or process isn't restored just by reverting the metadata that changed it.

questions.q: What is the difference between metadata rollback and data rollback, per this lesson?
options: They are the same thing described with two different names
Data rollback is always automatic on Salesforce, while metadata rollback requires a support ticket
Metadata rollback reverts configuration (fields, Flows, Apex) to its prior state; data rollback undoes changes already made to actual records, which depends on separate backup/recovery capability
Metadata rollback only applies to Apex, and data rollback only applies to Flows
questions.explain: These are genuinely separate problems: configuration can potentially be reverted, but records already changed by that configuration need their own recovery path, which may or may not exist.

questions.q: Per this lesson, when should a rollback plan be written?
options: After an incident has already started, improvised in real time
Before the change is approved and deployed, as part of what the CAB reviews
Only after the change has been in production for at least six months
Rollback plans are unnecessary if the change was declarative
questions.explain: The lesson's central discipline is that a rollback plan must be written and reviewed before deployment -- improvising one during an active incident is exactly the bad position advance planning is meant to avoid.

questions.q: What is a 'forward fix,' as described in this lesson?
options: Permanently disabling the entire release instead of fixing anything
A rule that prevents any future deployments from being approved
A type of Salesforce backup that runs automatically every night
Shipping a new, small, fast corrective change instead of reverting -- often faster and safer once other work has built on top of the risky change
questions.explain: A forward fix addresses the specific problem with a new corrective change rather than reverting, which is often the more practical option once later changes depend on the one causing the issue.

questions.q: Why does this lesson connect small, modular releases to easier rollback?
options: Smaller releases are always technically impossible to roll back
Modular releases eliminate the need for any rollback plan at all
Bundling many unrelated changes into one release makes a scoped reversal of just the problem component harder; smaller releases make a scoped reversal more realistic
Release size has no relationship to rollback difficulty
questions.explain: The lesson argues that keeping releases reasonably small and modular supports scoped reversal -- rolling back just the problematic piece -- rather than being forced to revert an entire release's worth of unrelated bundled changes.
